query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of zirconium (~0.2 at.%) to the uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will promote beneficial grain-boundary segregation and form ultrafine Zr-rich interfacial particles that stabilize the phase boundaries. This microalloying intervention is expected to enhance the alloy’s resistance to room-temperature creep, improve long-term mechanical performance under sustained loading and thermal cycling, and provide a more protective, stable oxide scale under corrosive conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with duplex FCC/B2 (or L12/B2) microstructure
generation.intervention: Minor microalloying addition of zirconium (≈0.2 atomic percent) during alloy preparation
generation.conditions: Performance evaluated under simulated fastener conditions including extreme temperature fluctuations (from room temperature up to ~700°C), long-term mechanical loading with room-temperature creep testing, and exposure to corrosive environments (e.g., chloride-containing solutions or molten salt for high-temperature corrosion tests)
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced segregation of Zr to phase boundaries and formation of fine Zr-rich interfacial particles that act as pinning sites
generation.mechanism: Zr is expected to segregate to the interphase boundaries in the eutectic structure, thereby reducing grain-boundary mobility and retarding creep deformation. The in situ formed Zr-rich nanoprecipitates at the interface can obstruct dislocation motion (increasing strength and work hardening) while simultaneously stabilizing the protective oxide scale during high-temperature exposure, improving corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the starting alloy, the Zr-modified EHEA is predicted to exhibit higher yield strength with improved room temperature creep resistance and long-term load performance, all while maintaining or slightly enhancing ductility. Improved corrosion resistance is also expected due to the improved stability of the surface oxide film.
generation.baseline: Properties of the as-cast, uniform fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA without Zr addition
generation.boundary: The efficacy is to be verified under laboratory simulated conditions that mimic fastener service environments (cyclic thermal exposures, sustained mechanical loading with creep tests, and corrosive media exposures). Results should be cautiously extrapolated to industrial scales given the potential for slight microstructural modifications outside the controlled processing window.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends the concept of minor alloying interventions reported for refractory metals (e.g., Mo) (see evidence: PMC11433366 and PMC6175879) by exploring the effect of a high-melting-point, grain-boundary active element (Zr) on creep and corrosion behavior. Uncertainty exists regarding whether Zr will segregate without forming brittle intermetallic phases in the unique eutectic microstructure and how its distribution will behave under extreme thermal cycling.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA samples with identical processing to develop the fine lamellar microstructure. In one set, incorporate 0.2 at.% Zr during melting. Subject both sets to identical post-processing heat treatments. Evaluate mechanical performance via long-term creep tests at room temperature, cyclic tensile/compression tests under simulated fastener loading conditions, and corrosion testing in chloride-containing environments and high-temperature molten salt tests.
measurements: Room-temperature creep strain rates over extended periods
Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility under cyclic loading
Corrosion rate and scale adhesion/spallation tests at elevated temperatures
Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM/EDS) to assess Zr segregation and interfacial particle formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-modified samples exhibit no statistically significant improvement (e.g., within 5% variation) in creep resistance, yield strength, and corrosion resistance compared to the baseline samples, or if they demonstrate any reduction in ductility or formation of deleterious brittle phases, then the hypothesis that minor Zr addition improves overall performance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA and co-doping Y and Hf AlCoCrFeNi2.1 YHf-EHEA coatings were successfully prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. 1. The YHf co-doping did not alter the solidification microstructure and phase structure of the EHEA coating. The microstructure morphologies of the top and bottom portions of coatings were composed of cellular and columnar dendrites, respectively. And the phase structure consisted of FCC and BCC/B2. 2. After heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h, the BCC/B2 structure was relatively stable in all coatings while the nanoscale Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC. 3. The grain sizes of the HT-EHEA and HT-YHf coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Additionally, the volume fractions of the LAGBs decreased by 13.9% and 8.3% in the HT-EHEA and HT-YHf coatings, respectively. 4. Al2O3 was found to be formed when the surface oxide products of the coatings were hot corroded at 900 °C for 60 h under Na2SO4 + 2

Because AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs present excellent properties, far beyond those of single-phase high entropy-alloys, they have been widely studied by scholars as new types of HEA. However, the current treatment methods for improving strength and toughness are relatively complicated, and how to further improve the properties is the key to developing these alloys. Alloying is a simple method that can effectively improve the mechanical properties and expand the application range of alloys. The majority of the additional elements in previous studies were metals, while few studies were performed on how high-melting-point elements and non-metallic elements affect the mechanical characteristics. Therefore, the aim of this work is to improve the strength and ductility of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA alloys by the alloying method. The influence of alloying components and their content on the microstructures and mechanical properties of the alloy were investigated by adding the refractory metal elements V and Mo and the non-metallic element B to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy. The results will provide theoretical guidance for the development of new high-strength and high-toughness eutectic high-entropy alloys.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Dislocation dominated plastic deformation in FCC phases
cited_evidence.text: Considering the much higher strength of BCC phase compared to that of FCC phase in the eutectic dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi HEA, the former served as the strengthening phase while the latter became the dominant carrier of deformation via dislocation plasticity, as evidenced by the in-situ deformation observations. At the early stage of deformation, plenty of dislocations were released from the phase boundary and glided along parallel slip bands, leading to the initial yielding. Despite of abundant dislocation sources, dislocation slips within the FCC phase became difficult due to the high lattice friction in HEAs, the intrinsic strengthening effect of multiple solution atoms, and therefore cross slip were activated by homogenous increase of strain accumulation. The interaction between primary slip arrays and cross-slip systems was to increase the rate of dislocation storage by forming dislocation substructures, and to further promote work hardening of the FCC phase. Meanwhile, the BCC phase was difficult to deform even at crack tips with high stress, as evidenced by the in situ deformation experiments shown in Fig. S3.
